h1: Microbrewery start-up costs: the lines founders forget
title: Start-Up Costs Founders Forget | Craft Beer School
desc: The cost lines new brewery founders overlook: water, drains, spares, licences, staff and working capital. A checklist to price before you borrow.
teaser: The brewhouse quote is the easy number. The surprises sit in drains, power, cold rooms, spares and the months before the first sale.
standfirst: Founders price the brewhouse and then run short on everything around it. Here are the lines that get forgotten, so you can price them before you borrow.
sections:
A quote for a brewhouse and fermenters is the start. Add the cold room, glycol chiller, compressed air, water treatment, boiler or steam, hoses, fittings and a cleaning station. Then the site works: floor drains, floor coatings, power upgrades and ventilation.

Ask each supplier what is not included. Freight, import duty, installation and commissioning are common gaps. See importing brewing equipment.

Ask for installation to be quoted separately from supply. Installation covers welding, pipework, electrics and plumbing. It often costs more than founders expect because a brewery is a plumbing project with a beer on the end.

Get at least two quotes for each major item and ask the suppliers to list their assumptions. A cheaper quote that leaves out the chiller, the controls or the delivery is not cheaper. Lay the quotes side by side in one sheet so the gaps show.

Check what warranty each supplier gives and who pays for spare parts after it ends. A brewhouse runs for years. The cost of keeping it running is part of the price.

Water treatment may be needed for chlorine removal, hardness or desalinated supply. Effluent rules can add a pre-treatment tank or a pH correction system. Ask the utility early and price what it requires.

A brewery also uses a lot of water. Track it from the first brew with this guide to water use per litre.

Meter the water supply on day one. If you do not know how much you use, you cannot spot a leak or a wasteful cleaning cycle. Effluent is often charged on top of the water in, so waste costs twice.

Licences cost money and time. The costs vary by country. Add company formation, lawyers, insurance, fire and building approvals, signage and a deposit on the lease. If you run a taproom, add furniture, glassware, a till and a sound system you can afford.

Insurance deserves a careful conversation with a broker. Product liability, property, stock in tank and business interruption are different covers. Ask what happens if a fermenter fails and the beer is lost.

Budget a first stock of spare pump seals, gaskets, sensors and cleaning chemicals. Add a small lab: a hydrometer or density meter, pH meter, thermometer and a microscope if you can run yeast counts. Those are modest sums compared to a dumped batch.

Add the cost of your first few brews that go wrong. Every brewery has them. A budget with no allowance for dumped beer is a budget that has not met reality.

This is the line founders forget most. Beer takes weeks to brew and condition before anything sells. You pay for malt, hops, staff and rent for months before income arrives. Customers may then take 30 to 60 days to pay. Plan enough cash to cover the gap, plus a reserve.

A realistic demand forecast tells you how long that gap lasts.
Staff and marketing before the first sale

People cost money before beer does. A brewer, a packaging hand and a manager may be on the payroll for weeks or months before the first invoice goes out. Add training, uniforms, safety equipment and the cost of recruiting.

Marketing starts early too. A name that is trademarked, a simple website, labels or tap badges, photography and a launch event all cost money before you earn any. Keep the launch modest and put the saving into a longer cash runway.

If you have never run a brewery, buy time with advice. A few days with an experienced brewer during commissioning saves more than it costs.

Make a single costing sheet: equipment, site works, licences, stock, staff before sales and a contingency. Compare it with the models in brewpub or production brewery and in opening a brewpub in a new country.

Then ask a second person to find what is missing.

Show your lender the sheet and the assumptions behind it. A founder who can explain every line gets taken more seriously than one who points to a round number. See what investors ask a brewery founder.
faqs: How much contingency should I add?
A common practice is to hold a reserve on top of the quoted costs and to raise it when equipment is imported. Agree the figure with a lender or adviser who knows your market.
Do I need to buy new equipment?
Not always. Used kit can cut costs, but it needs inspection and a clear record of repairs. Price spares and commissioning either way.
What is the most common missing cost?
Working capital. Founders plan for the equipment and then run short while the first beer is still in the tank.

cta.title: Price the whole brewery, not just the brewhouse
cta.body: Brewery Business Management is a live three-week course on costing, pricing, forecasting, licensing steps and the figures a lender will want to see. Classes are live online on Saturdays and Sundays, 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM India Standard Time, so you join from your own time zone and recordings cover any class you miss. It shows how to build a start-up costing that includes the lines founders forget.
